artifacts.layman_summary: Checks whether a popular table of water's boiling point by altitude was measured or calculated, and how a simple pressure model compares. The table drifts from the model above about 4.5 km; no independent measurements were found to settle it.
artifacts.name: gen_art_research_1
artifacts.summary: This round tested the Engineering ToolBox water-boiling-point-versus-altitude table. The page states no method, formula, steam table or measured dataset, so its provenance is unknown [1]. Its sea-level and altitude rows (for example 100.0 C at 0 m and 71.1 C at 9144 m) were relayed by a summarising fetch and must be checked against the page. Using the standard ISA pressure curve and a constant-enthalpy Clausius-Clapeyron model (40.65 kJ/mol anchored at 373.124 K), the table agrees with the model to within about 0.35 K up to 4.6 km. Above that the table runs higher: about +0.8 K at 6.1 km, +1.7 K at 7.6 km, +2.6 K at 8.8 km and +2.8 K at 9.1 km. This residual pattern is a computed result from the relayed values, not a published finding. It is consistent with a table built on a different thermodynamic or pressure assumption, but it does not identify which. No independent measured boiling-point dataset with station pressure was found, so the question of how well the barometric model predicts measurements is not answered. Summit estimates in the sources cluster at 68 to 72 C [4][5], and these are calculations, not observations. Keene (1995) in the Journal of Chemical Education was not located after two rounds of search. The only related altitude-boiling article found (ACS DOI 10.1021/ed067p45) returned HTTP 403, so its content is unverified [2]. The IAPWS-95 saturation table in NIST NISTIR 5078 could not be parsed by the fetch tool, so the IAPWS reference step is incomplete. Pressure-boiling values in the Wikipedia vapour-pressure article are tied to a Wagner-Pruss/IAPWS-based correlation, and its 100 C row corresponds to about 101.4 kPa [3]. Confidence: high that the ToolBox page states no method; moderate on the residual pattern (depends on transcription); low on any claim about measurement agreement, because none was found. What would change this: a readable IAPWS saturation table to compare with, and at least two measured station-pressure datasets reaching above 8 km.
artifacts.title: Checking a Boiling-Point Altitude Table Against Physics

artifacts.layman_summary: A cited table of water boiling temperatures at different altitudes, with a model-computed reference and a published benchmark, but no direct measurements yet.
artifacts.name: gen_art_dataset_1
artifacts.summary: This artifact is a reference table for testing how well the simple barometric formula predicts the boiling point of water at altitude. The table has 250 rows from two sources, each labelled by data_type. The first source is the Engineering ToolBox 'Water - Boiling Points vs. Altitude' table, taken as published: 125 rows with altitude and boiling temperature, marked computed_unknown_method because the page does not state its method. The second source is 125 IAPWS-IF97 saturation rows, computed with the iapws Python package v1.5.5 at ISA standard-atmosphere pressures for the same altitudes, marked computed_reference. The table contains zero measured rows. The planned measured sources, Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings 1939 and the CRC Handbook table, were located as NIST and other records, but their tables could not be transcribed reliably from the fetched text, so no measured row was added. The plan's rule against padding the measured set means the downstream residual test by altitude band has no measured points to report. A key check: the ToolBox values agree with IAPWS-at-ISA to within -0.31 to +1.94 K over 125 altitudes (median +0.02 K), so the benchmark is most likely computed from a standard atmosphere and is not independent evidence. Files: data.py builds full_data_out.json in the exp_sel_data_out format, grouped by source; mini_data_out.json and preview_data_out.json are the reduced variants; the table build and validation scripts sit beside them. The full file passes schema validation with zero errors and is well under the size limit.
artifacts.title: Water boiling point versus pressure reference table

artifacts.layman_summary: We compute how water's boiling point drops with altitude using four simple air-pressure and steam models, and compare each with a published table. The simplest shortcut stays closest; no measured data could be verified.
artifacts.name: gen_art_experiment_1
artifacts.summary: This artifact computes the boiling point of water from 0 to 9 km in a 2x2 factorial design: atmosphere model (isothermal barometric formula versus ISA lapse-rate) crossed with thermodynamic model (constant-enthalpy Clausius-Clapeyron anchored at 373.15 K versus the IAPWS-IF97 saturation curve). Residuals (model minus the Engineering ToolBox table, in K) are reported by band (0-3, 3-6, 6-9 km) as bias, mean absolute error and maximum absolute error. Against the table, the isothermal and constant-enthalpy variant (V1) has bias +0.23, +0.51 and +0.50 K across the three bands and stays within 0.6 K everywhere. The ISA variant with constant enthalpy (V3) drifts to -1.64 K bias in the 6-9 km band, with a maximum error of 2.6 K. The two residual differences V1-V3 and V2-V4 never change sign over 0-9 km, so no crossover altitude exists. The V1-V2 difference grows with altitude, consistent with the expected behaviour of the constant-enthalpy shortcut. Sensitivity runs vary the enthalpy by ±500 J/mol and sea-level pressure by ±1 kPa. The IAPWS-IF97 normal boiling point is 373.124 K (99.974 °C); the constant-enthalpy formula gives 100.00 °C at sea level. No independently measured boiling-point and station-pressure pairs could be verified, so the measured comparison is empty and no conclusion is drawn about accuracy against measurement; the Engineering ToolBox table is a reference curve of unstated method, not a measurement. An independent re-derivation of all band statistics matches the stored values to 2.5e-13 K. Outputs: results/ (predictions, residuals, band summaries, sensitivity, sanity checks, figure), method_out.json with full, mini and preview variants, and reproducibility.md.
artifacts.title: Boiling point vs altitude: four model variants

critiques.description: The research question asks how well the barometric formula predicts measured boiling points. The record contains zero measured pairs (measured_comparison.json n_points = 0; measured_pairs.csv has only a header). The run answers a model-versus-computed-table question, so coverage of the original request is partial, and the title question has no answer in this iteration.
critiques.suggested_action: State in the opening section that the measured comparison was not carried out and that the question is unanswered. Make the next iteration's primary task to obtain at least two measured boiling-point and station-pressure sets (Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings 1939 values, or a measured dataset above 8 km), with each row's source page recorded.

critiques.description: The hypothesis clauses are judged 'holds' or 'does not hold' against the Engineering ToolBox table. Table 3 shows that table is within 0.31 K of an IAPWS-at-ISA calculation at all 70 altitudes below 5 km (recomputed). The 'holds' verdicts therefore measure agreement with a computed curve, not accuracy. The report says this in one paragraph but still scores the clauses as passed.
critiques.suggested_action: Rewrite the clause verdicts as 'consistent with the computed reference' and remove the words 'holds' and 'passed' for accuracy claims. Carry the Table 3 caveat into the verdict itself, not only into the discussion.

critiques.description: Table 4 is presented as an independent match between the research artifact and the experiment. Both use the same constant-enthalpy ISA model, and the research artifact's summary says the ISA constants were 'written from memory' with no source. The agreement therefore shows the same formula was implemented twice, not that the residual has been corroborated. The report does not mention the unsourced constants.
critiques.suggested_action: Add the 'from memory' disclosure from research_out.json to the Table 4 paragraph. Describe the agreement as a code-level consistency check. Source the ISA lapse-rate and pressure constants to a cited standard and recompute the research values from code.

critiques.description: The research artifact's residuals exist only in its summary text, not in an output file. The report acknowledges this, but Table 4's 8.8-9.1 km row claims a match that cannot be made: the experiment's residual grid ends at 8992 m (recomputed: V3 -2.605 K there), and the 9144 m value of +2.8 has no experiment counterpart. The row therefore reports agreement for a point the experiment never computed.
critiques.suggested_action: Either evaluate the experiment at 9144 m and add it to the comparison, or restrict the Table 4 match to 8992 m and label the 9.1 km research value as unmatched. Write the research artifact's residuals to a file so they can be recomputed.

critiques.description: The positive finding that the ToolBox table is most likely a standard-atmosphere calculation (within 0.31 K below 5 km of IAPWS-at-ISA) is not compared with any published neighbour. The nearest neighbours are Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings (1939) for measured vapour pressure, and the IAPWS-95 formulation [2] for the thermodynamic reference, which the run did not evaluate against its own IAPWS-95 check. The record does not say what this iteration adds beyond them.
critiques.suggested_action: Add a short comparison: name the nearest published measured and formulated references for boiling temperature versus pressure, and state that the new contribution is a provenance check of this specific table (computed versus measured), not a new physical result.

critiques.description: The Artifact 1 section says the 373.124 K versus 373.15 K anchor difference 'shifts absolute values by a few hundredths of a kelvin and does not change the pattern'. This was never run. A 0.026 K shift is about 5-10% of the V1 biases (0.23-0.50 K), so it is not obviously negligible, and the later Dead ends section concedes the anchor effect was not separated.
critiques.suggested_action: Either run the experiment with the 373.124 K anchor and report the change in Table 1, or delete the claim that the pattern is unchanged.

critiques.description: The conclusion 'The Engineering ToolBox table is not a measurement, on the evidence of this iteration' is stated more firmly in 'What we have learned' than in the body, which says 'most likely computed' and that the method is not shown. The summary is a provenance inference from agreement, not a demonstration.
critiques.suggested_action: Use 'most likely computed from a standard atmosphere' in the summary to match the body text.

critiques.description: The run's verification artifacts are not recorded in the report: audit_rederive.py (independent re-derivation matching to 2.5e-13 K, with the caveat that the iapws library itself is not independently verified), the research_verification.json result (valid, but passages = [] so no quoted claim was checked), and the sanity checks passing. These belong in the record.
critiques.suggested_action: Add a 'Verification' subsection to the iteration listing each check, what it confirms, and what it does not confirm (in particular that research_verification.json checked no passages).

critiques.description: The research artifact's low-altitude residuals (about +0.03 K at 0 m and -0.1 K at 1.5-2.1 km as table minus model) and its Wikipedia check (100 C at about 101.4 kPa) are not in the report. Table 4 starts at 4.3 km, so the reader cannot see whether the two artifacts agree at low altitude.
critiques.suggested_action: Extend Table 4 down to 0 m, or add a sentence giving the low-altitude research values and the matching experiment values (V3 is +0.11 K as a 0-3 km band bias, which is consistent once the sign convention is reversed).

critiques.description: The report's sub-band values and Table 1 cells are not accompanied by sample sizes or by the altitudes that define each band. The experiment grid has 119 altitudes (40/39/40 per band), and the report mentions this only in passing.
critiques.suggested_action: State n for every band in Table 1 and Table 2, and list the altitude grid (0-8992 m, step about 76 m) in the Strategy section.

dimension_scores.justification: The computed numbers are correct and the experiment's internal checks pass. The soundness deduction comes from interpretation: hypothesis clauses are passed or failed against a benchmark that is nearly a standard-atmosphere calculation, and the cross-artifact 'reproduction' of the research residuals rests on a shared model with constants the research artifact says were written from memory.

The chronology is clear, one iteration section, and each table is introduced by what it settles. Several tables lack the sample size n, and the Table 4 rows are not matched to the research artifact's full stated values.

The central question, how the formula compares with published measured boiling points, is unanswered. The iteration records the absence of data and the model-versus-table comparison, which is useful, but the run preserves no measured benchmark and no measurement-based accuracy result.

review.overall_assessment: The record is largely traceable and its arithmetic holds. I recomputed Table 1 (all 12 cells, bias/MAE/max), Table 2 (sub-band means from residuals.json: V1 +0.09/+0.30, V2 +0.09/+0.40, V3 +0.08/+0.14, V4 +0.08/+0.24), Table 3 (125 ToolBox-minus-IAPWS differences: range -0.31 to +1.94 K, median +0.02 K, 70 altitudes below 5 km within 0.31 K), the Table 4 experiment column (V3 at 4267/4648/6096/7620/8916/8992 m: -0.16/-0.27/-0.80/-1.65/-2.53/-2.60 K), and spot-checked Table 5 rows. Sanity checks, the empty measured comparison and the sensitivity grid are all recorded honestly, and dead ends (Keene 1995, Osborne/CRC transcription, NIST table parsing, the ACS 403) are kept with their evidence. Headline numbers come from executed artifacts, so results_reported is true. The weaknesses are scope and interpretation. The question asks how the barometric formula compares with published measurements, and the run has no measured row, so the record answers only a model-versus-computed-table question. The hypothesis clauses are then judged against a benchmark that the report's own Table 3 shows is nearly identical to a standard-atmosphere IAPWS calculation, so those verdicts are not independent accuracy evidence. The research artifact's residuals are presented as a reproduction even though both sides share the same constant-enthalpy ISA model, and the research artifact's ISA constants were written from memory. That disclosure is missing from the report. Coverage of the original request is partial.
strengths: Every number I recomputed from the experiment's residuals.json and summary_by_band.json matches the report to the stated rounding, including Table 1 (all 12 cells), Table 2 sub-bands and the V3 values in Table 4.

Table 3 is recomputed exactly from full_data_out.json: 125 paired altitudes, range -0.31 to +1.94 K, median +0.02 K, and 70 altitudes below 5 km. The report correctly concludes the benchmark is not independent evidence.

The sensitivity analysis (Table 5) is a strong piece of work. It shows that a 1 kPa change in sea-level pressure moves the bands by about 0.25 K and a 500 J/mol change in enthalpy moves the 6-9 km bias by about 0.27 K, and the report draws the right consequence: the 0.6 K criterion holds only for the stated constants.

Dead ends and blocked steps are recorded with their causes: the Keene search, the unparsed NIST table, the untranscribed Osborne and CRC values, and the HTTP 403 on the ACS DOI. Nothing was silently dropped.
The sign convention difference between the research artifact (table minus model) and the experiment (model minus table) is flagged and reconciled, and the anchor difference is named as unresolved.

strategies.expected_outcome: After this iteration: a provenance note on the Engineering ToolBox table (measured or computed), a cited and typed table of measured boiling-point and pressure pairs, and predictions and residuals for the four variants against the benchmark table, by altitude band. The head-to-head comparison against measured values and the verdict on the hypothesis follow in iteration 2.
strategies.objective: Find which approximation sets the error in the simple barometric boiling-point model. Compare a 2x2 set of atmospheric and thermodynamic variants against the Engineering ToolBox table and against independently measured boiling points from 0 to 9 km.
strategies.rationale: The hypothesis rests on two inputs that are not yet established: the Engineering ToolBox table has no stated method, and the intended measured benchmark (Keene 1995) has not been located. This iteration fixes both inputs and computes all four predictions, so the next iteration can run the decisive comparison against measurement. Shift within the question: the user asked how well the simple formula predicts measured boiling points. This strategy asks which step produces the error, which is the nearest version of that question the current evidence can answer positively.

artifacts.layman_summary: This artifact tries to test how well simple air-pressure formulas predict the boiling temperature of water at altitude against real measurements. No usable measured data could be obtained this round, so it reports that no accuracy claim can be made.
artifacts.name: gen_art_experiment_2
artifacts.summary: Experiment artifact for the question: how well does the simple barometric formula predict the boiling point of water at altitude, compared with published measurements? The plan transcribes measured boiling-temperature and pressure pairs from Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings (1939) and the CRC Handbook, then compares four model variants (isothermal or ISA pressure, each inverted to boiling temperature by a constant-enthalpy Clausius-Clapeyron step or by IAPWS-IF97 saturation) by altitude band. In this round the measured set is EMPTY: the NIST RP1229 PDF returned no readable table text, the CRC Handbook table was not obtained, and Keene (1995) was not located. No row was padded from computed tables. The output is therefore labelled untested, with the statement: no measured comparison; no accuracy claim; computed reference shown only as context. The computed context uses the 250-row reference table (125 Engineering ToolBox rows and 125 IAPWS-IF97 at ISA pressure rows), which is not measured data. Unit checks pass: IAPWS-IF97 at 101.325 kPa gives 373.1243 K, the ISA and isothermal pressure formulas return their expected values, and all four variants agree with 373.124 K at sea-level pressure within 0.05 K. On the computed reference, the constant-enthalpy ISA variant (V3) runs about 1.7 K below the ToolBox values at 6 km and above (n = 42, bias -1.72 K; independently re-derived as -1.716 K, and a shuffled-label placebo does not reproduce it). Moving the anchor from 373.124 K to 373.15 K shifts V1 and V3 by about +0.024 K. Outputs are full, mini and preview JSON files, band statistics, per-row residuals, a source log with zero rows retained, and reproducibility notes with pinned dependencies. The high-altitude question (6 to 9 km) remains unanswered because no measured rows exist there.
artifacts.title: Checking boiling-point formulas against measured data

artifacts.layman_summary: Checks whether a simple altitude-pressure model predicts the boiling point of water, using measured data at high altitude; no usable measurements were found, so the result is a null outcome.
artifacts.name: gen_art_experiment_3
artifacts.summary: This artifact tests a barometric plus constant-enthalpy model of water's boiling point against measured boiling temperatures paired with station pressure, focusing on altitudes above 5 km. It implements a 2x2 set of variants: an isothermal or ISA (standard atmosphere) pressure path, crossed with a constant-enthalpy Clausius-Clapeyron or IAPWS-97 saturation thermodynamic model. Unit checks pass: the Clausius-Clapeyron and IAPWS-97 models give 373.124 K at 101325 Pa, the ISA altitude inversion round-trips to 1e-11 m, and the ISA pressure at 11 km is 22632.6 Pa. A bounded search of two query rounds (Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings 1939; high-altitude station and summit records; Keene 1995) found the NIST RP1229 paper but no transcribable measured boiling-temperature-versus-pressure rows, none above 5 km, and no retrievable Keene 1995 text. The measured set is therefore empty (n = 0) for every band, and no residual statistics are reported. This is a null outcome, not a finding: the question of how well the barometric model predicts measured boiling points at altitude is untested. Computed checks, labelled as not measured evidence, were run on the reference dataset of the upstream artifact art_39-uxNptYM5-. The IAPWS-97 variant at ISA pressures reproduces the stored computed rows to 0.00094 K. The Engineering ToolBox table, of unstated method, differs from the models by a bias of +0.37 K for the isothermal Clausius-Clapeyron variant, -0.65 K for the ISA Clausius-Clapeyron variant, and -0.30 K for the ISA IAPWS variant. Anchor sensitivity (373.15 K) shifts the Clausius-Clapeyron variants by about +0.02 K, and a plus or minus 500 J/mol change in the enthalpy of vaporization by about 0.17 K. An independent re-derivation through a separate code path (IAPWS-97 backward equation P to T, inline ISA pressure, raw JSON rows) reproduced all headline numbers. Deviations from the plan: the IAPWS solve bracket was set to 273.16 to 647.0 K, because the plan's upper bound of 373.946 K is not the critical point and does not bracket the saturation pressure. Limitations: no measured comparison was performed at any altitude, and no uncertainty intervals are given because no residuals exist.
artifacts.title: Boiling point of water vs altitude: measured test

artifacts.layman_summary: Checks a simple altitude formula for water's boiling point against a computed reference table, and separates how much of the error comes from the pressure model versus the thermodynamic assumptions.
artifacts.name: gen_art_experiment_4
artifacts.summary: This artifact attributes the residual of a barometric boiling-point model of water to two causes. It crosses two pressure models (isothermal and ISA troposphere) with four thermodynamic variants: constant enthalpy anchored at 373.124 K, constant enthalpy anchored at 373.15 K, an effective constant enthalpy fitted to IAPWS-IF97 saturation, and direct IAPWS-IF97 saturation inversion. Residuals are taken against two computed reference series from the dataset dependency: the Engineering ToolBox table (method not stated) and IAPWS-IF97 saturation at ISA pressures. No measured boiling points are used, so every result is an agreement statistic against a computed reference, not an accuracy claim against measurement. Per-altitude residuals and band statistics (n, bias, MAE, max absolute error) are reported for 0-3, 3-6 and 6-9 km (the 6-9 km band includes 9144 m). Headline values for 6-9 km against the ToolBox table are: isothermal bias +0.47 to +1.10 K, ISA bias -1.03 to -1.72 K, depending on variant. The anchor shift (373.124 vs 373.15 K) is about -0.023 K, a minor term. The enthalpy treatment removes about 37-40% of the ISA 6-9 km bias, and increases the isothermal bias. The atmosphere effect (ISA minus isothermal) is about -2.2 K at 6-9 km and dominates the residual; no sign change occurs over 0-9144 m. Implementation checks (sea-level inversion within 3e-4 K, ISA reproduction of the IAPWS reference within 5.3e-4 K, plain-loop statistics matching to 1e-9 K) pass. An independent re-derivation from the raw residual rows reproduces the headline numbers. Limitations: the effective enthalpy is fitted to the same IAPWS curve as the reference, so it is not independent; the result describes the standard atmosphere only; and the dependency contains no measured rows.
artifacts.title: Splitting boiling-point model error by cause

critiques.description: Coverage of the original request is partial. The request asks how well the barometric formula predicts measured boiling points. After two iterations the measured comparison is still empty (measured_pairs.csv has no data rows; measured_records.json is []; sources_summary.json n_measured = 0). Iteration 2 spent three experiment artifacts on computed references: art_Dwo3Mclnlbtv largely repeats the V1 to V4 band numbers of art_e7cQzFbFiEBS against the same ToolBox table, and the attribution split is a decomposition of a non-measured reference. The report says 'three routes remain untried in full' while also recording two failed rounds of search, which is an inconsistency about what was actually attempted.
critiques.suggested_action: Make the next iteration's only primary task the acquisition of measured sets, and add a per-route retrieval log (URL or record ID, fetch result, rows obtained) for each source tried: Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings 1939; the CRC table; Keene 1995; NIST RP1229; a summit or station record above 8 km. Do not add further computed-reference decomposition until a measured row exists. Reword the 'untried' statement so it matches the attempt log.

critiques.description: The benchmark's provenance is not verified in the record. The art_meMsxdA1r_bm summary states that the ToolBox sea-level and altitude rows 'were relayed by a summarising fetch and must be checked against the page', and gives the residual confidence as 'moderate ... depends on transcription'. The report never records that check. All band statistics in Tables 1, 2, 7 and 9, and the -2.77 K and -2.63 K point values, depend on those 125 transcribed rows, yet the verification section of Iteration 2 does not mention the transcription.
critiques.suggested_action: Add a 'Benchmark transcription' check to the Iteration 2 verification section. Either re-fetch the ToolBox page and compare the 125 rows with full_data_out.json (record the number of matching rows and any mismatches), or state in the Table 1, 7 and 9 captions that all band values are conditional on an unverified transcription.

critiques.description: A comparative claim contradicts the report's own Table 8. The 'Reading this iteration' section says that against the IAPWS-at-ISA reference 'the isothermal model is less accurate than the ISA model at every band'. Table 8 gives 0-3 km: isothermal V1 bias +0.020 K (MAE 0.036 K) versus ISA V3 bias -0.093 K (MAE 0.093 K). The isothermal model is closer at 0-3 km, and the statement is false for that band. The contradiction is in a clause the report uses to rank the two atmospheres.
critiques.suggested_action: Correct the sentence to say the isothermal model is closer at 0-3 km (bias and MAE) and less close at 3 km and above. Note that this reversal is expected, because the reference is itself an ISA calculation, so the near-surface agreement reflects the reference's construction rather than the physics.

critiques.description: The positive claim that the ToolBox table is 'most likely a computed standard-atmosphere calculation below 5 km' has no published neighbour named. The Responses section names Osborne, Stimson and Ginnings (1939), which the run did not transcribe, and the IAPWS-95 formulation [2], which the run did not check against its saturation table. Neither is a published boiling-point-versus-altitude table, so the report does not say whether any published altitude table is itself a computed table, nor what this iteration adds to that literature beyond one table's provenance.
critiques.suggested_action: Search for published boiling-point-versus-altitude or pressure-boiling tables (handbook tables, standard-atmosphere textbook tables, and the Keene 1995 compilation if it can be found) and state for each whether its method is stated. Then state the new contribution precisely: a provenance check of one specific table with a computed reference, which is a benchmark-audit result rather than a physical result.

critiques.description: The Iteration 2 section misquotes Iteration 1. It says 'Iteration 1 stated that the table lies within 0.31 K of the IAPWS-at-ISA calculation at all altitudes below 5 km'. Iteration 1 actually reported that the difference runs from -0.31 K to +1.94 K across all 125 rows, with a median of +0.02 K. The 0.31 K below-5-km figure is a new Iteration 2 result, but it is presented as a restatement.
critiques.suggested_action: Correct the restatement in place in Iteration 2 (say 'Iteration 1 reported a range of -0.31 to +1.94 K over all 125 rows; restricting to the 70 rows below 5 km, the range is -0.31 to +0.11 K'), and mark the change as a correction rather than an earlier claim.

critiques.description: Iteration 1's altitude grid is described inconsistently. The Iteration 1 Strategy and Table 1 imply 119 altitudes from 0 to 8992 m (40/39/40 per band). The residuals.json header reads 'table altitudes 0-9000 m'. Iteration 2 then describes the 119-point grid as '0 to 8992 m, step about 76 m, plus 9144 m', which would make 120 points and conflicts with the band counts.
critiques.suggested_action: State the exact altitude list used in Iteration 1 (count and endpoints, from residuals.json comparison_grid), and correct the Iteration 2 description so the 9144 m point is either included in or excluded from that grid consistently.

critiques.description: Table 4 is still the Iteration 1 table. The research side has no file and is read from text, and the experiment column has not been extended to 8992 m and 9144 m in the table itself. The 9.1 km match is handled only in Iteration 2's 'Responses to the review' prose, so anyone reading the table alone sees the mismatch unresolved. The research artifact's values are also attributed in Iteration 2 to 'as the reviewer records' rather than to the artifact (research_report.md or research_out.json), which holds the same statement.
critiques.suggested_action: Write the research artifact's residuals to a file, or cite research_report.md directly for the values. Add the 8992 m and 9144 m experiment rows to Table 4 with their anchor noted, and label the 9.1 km research value as unmatched if it is not at a computed altitude.

critiques.description: The Iteration 2 claim that the experiments used the dataset altitudes 'as the plan permits when the grid differs' cites a plan permission that is not quoted anywhere in the record. The change of altitude set also alters the band sizes and makes Iteration 1 and Iteration 2 numbers not directly comparable, which the report notes only in passing.
critiques.suggested_action: Quote the plan clause that permits the change, or state that the change was made without a plan clause. Give a one-line table comparing the Iteration 1 and Iteration 2 altitude sets and their band counts.

critiques.description: The closing 'What we have learned' section draws an error-attribution conclusion that the body does not support: 'The atmosphere term, not the thermodynamic step, is the larger error against this table.' The body states that the table's method above 5 km is not identified and that the table is a benchmark of unknown method. The conclusion holds only for that table and cannot be read as an error attribution for the physics.
critiques.suggested_action: Restate the sentence as 'against the ToolBox table, the atmosphere term is about three times the thermodynamic term at 6-9 km; because the table's method above 5 km is unidentified, this is not an attribution of physical error'.

critiques.description: The verification section relies on a reviewer's reading of the research artifact ('as the reviewer records from its research_out.json; that file was not re-read in this pass'), although the file is in the workspace. The same applies to the passages list in research_verification.json. The disclosure is correct, but the claim can be checked directly and should be checked rather than attributed to the review.
critiques.suggested_action: Open iter_1/gen_art/gen_art_research_1/research_out.json and research_verification.json, quote the 'written from memory' sentence and the passages field, and cite the artifact in the verification entry.

dimension_scores.justification: Computed-reference numbers are traceable and reproduce, and the attribution arithmetic is correct. But one comparative claim contradicts its own Table 8 (isothermal is closer than ISA at 0-3 km against IAPWS-at-ISA), the benchmark's transcription is unverified, and the closing summary states the atmosphere-versus-thermodynamic conclusion for a table whose method above 5 km the body says is not identified. The headline question is not tested against any measurement.

The record can be followed in order, each iteration has a strategy and a reasoning account, and tables are introduced by what they test. Some cross-references are muddled, for example Table 4 is still the Iteration 1 table with the 9.1 km row unmatched, and the closing summary is rewritten in place rather than appended.

The report preserves all six executed artifacts' main tables and the empty measured results, and records the failed measured searches. It omits several items that the artifacts record: the benchmark transcription caveat, a shuffled-label placebo, the IAPWS bracket deviation from the plan, and the summary-level headline biases of the measured-test artifact that differ slightly from Table 9.

review.overall_assessment: The record is honest about its central gap: after two iterations it contains zero measured boiling-point and station-pressure pairs, so the question in the title (how well the barometric formula predicts measured boiling points) is still unanswered. Everything reported is an agreement statistic against a Engineering ToolBox table whose method is unstated, plus a computed IAPWS-at-ISA reference. I recomputed the headline numbers from the executed artifacts: the Table 7, 8 and 9 band statistics match band_stats.csv and band_summary.json; the Table 3 claim that 70 rows below 5 km lie between -0.31 and +0.11 K from IAPWS-at-ISA (median -0.17 K) matches per_row_residuals.csv; the -2.77 K value at 9144 m and -2.63 K at 8992 m match; and the decomposition in Table 10 is arithmetically correct. So results_reported is true. However, the record has a real contradiction (a claim that the isothermal model is less accurate than the ISA model 'at every band' against IAPWS-at-ISA, which Table 8 itself refutes at 0-3 km), it never records that the 125 benchmark rows were transcribed from a summarising fetch and not checked against the page, and it leaves the nearest-neighbour check for its positive provenance claim undone. Its conclusions about the table's method and about which term dominates the error are stated more firmly in the closing summary than the body supports. Soundness is fair rather than poor because the computed-reference arithmetic is traceable and correct; the coverage gap is the dominant problem for the run's original question.
strengths: Explicitly states that the measured comparison is empty and that the title question is unanswered, and does not dress a computed-reference agreement up as accuracy against measurement.

Every headline band table (Tables 1, 2, 7, 8, 9) traces to a named output file, and the values I recomputed or spot-checked match: for example Table 7 V1 6 km and above +0.470 K (n = 42) and V3 -1.716 K match band_stats.csv and band_summary.json.

The Table 10 decomposition (atmosphere effect about -2.19 K, thermodynamic effect about +0.63 to +0.69 K at 6-9 km) and the 38-40 percent reduction in the ISA bias reproduce from Table 9 and the band summary.
Iteration 2 corrects several Iteration 1 claims in the body and openly reverses the earlier conclusion that the thermodynamic step carries most of the high-altitude error, with the evidence shown.
Dead ends are recorded with their evidence (measured_pairs.csv and measured_records.json both empty, NIST RP1229 table text unreadable, Keene 1995 not located, IAPWS-95 table unparsed).

strategies.expected_outcome: After this final iteration: a measured boiling-temperature table at low altitude with a citation per row and n per band; a second measured table at high altitude, or a recorded statement that none could be cited; the four variants' bias and maximum error against each measured set; and an attribution of the residual to the anchor, the enthalpy approximation, or the lapse rate, with the Engineering ToolBox table reported only as a computed reference.
strategies.objective: Establish how well the simple barometric boiling-point model predicts independently measured boiling temperatures against station pressure, from sea level to above 8 km, and attribute any residual to the atmospheric step (isothermal versus ISA lapse rate) or the thermodynamic step (constant versus temperature-dependent enthalpy). The novel contribution is a measured-pair test of this specific model chain, with the Engineering ToolBox table labelled as a computed reference rather than a measurement.
strategies.rationale: This is the final iteration of the run (2 of 2), so the measured comparison, which is the user's actual question, has to be completed inside this round. Artifacts planned in one round run in parallel and cannot depend on each other, so each measured-comparison experiment must acquire its own measured pairs, cite each row, and run variants V1 to V4 against them. The shift within the question is from a model-versus-computed-table test to a model-versus-measurement test, which is the nearest version of the user's question the run can still answer in one round. The attribution experiment deepens the thermodynamic step on the computed reference, so the paper can say which assumption carries the error, not only that an error exists.
strategies.title: Measured boiling points test the barometric model
